a: in the tenth month
t: The dates of the siege and the fall
p: The siege began in January 588 BC by the usual count; the city fell in July 586. Some scholars date the fall to 587.
b: Jeremiah gives the same dates as 2 Kings: the siege begins in Zedekiah's ninth year, the tenth month (see 2 Kings 25:1 for the day and for the fast days that keep these dates), and the wall is breached in his eleventh year, fourth month. This site counts the fall as 586 BC, as its 2 Kings does. Scholars who count Zedekiah's years by a spring-to-spring calendar, or who date Nebuchadnezzar's reign differently, reach 587. The two sides use the same biblical numbers and differ over how the Judean calendar ran; the difference does not change the order of events. The Babylonian Chronicle for these years is lost, so no Babylonian text gives the day Jerusalem fell.

a: the city was breached
t: The ninth of Tammuz and the seventeenth
p: The Mishnah puts the breach of the wall on the 17th of Tammuz; Jeremiah gives the 9th.
b: The fast of the Seventeenth of Tammuz, which opens the three weeks before the Ninth of Av, is tied in the Mishnah to the breaching of the city wall (Mishnah Taanit 4:6). Jeremiah and 2 Kings both say the ninth day of the fourth month. The Talmud notices the difference and explains it by two different breaches, the first Temple's and the second's (see Bavli Taanit 28b). Whatever one makes of that answer, the fast of the fourth month named in Zechariah 8:19 is the one remembered here.
r: Mishnah Taanit 4:6; Bavli Taanit 28b; Zechariah 8:19; 2 Kings 25:3–4; Jeremiah 52:6–7

a: Nergal-sharezer of Samgar
t: The Babylonian officers at the Middle Gate
p: Four of the names fit Babylonian officials, and a tablet found in the British Museum names one of them.
b: The list is hard to divide, because the Hebrew runs the names together. Read here: Nergal-sharezer of Samgar, Nebo-sarsekim the Rab-saris ("chief court officer"), and a second Nergal-sharezer, the Rab-mag. "Samgar" may be a place or a Babylonian office (simmagir), and the meaning of "Rab-mag" is uncertain. The second Nergal-sharezer is often identified with Neriglissar, Nebuchadnezzar's son-in-law, who ruled Babylon in 560–556 BC, though the name was common. In 2007 the British Museum announced a Babylonian tablet dated to Nebuchadnezzar's tenth year (595 BC) that records gold sent to the temple Esangila by "Nabu-sharrussu-ukin, the chief eunuch," the Akkadian title behind the Hebrew Rab-saris. The British Museum's catalogue treats him as the same man as Nebo-sarsekim, and the identification is widely accepted; the Hebrew "Sarsekim" looks like a garbling of the second part of the name. Verse 13 names a Rab-saris "Nebushazban"; the two names are probably spellings of one officer, since each list has one Rab-saris, but the Hebrew does not say so. Swete's printed Greek writes all these names differently again.

a: he pronounced sentence on him
p: Zedekiah had sworn loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar in God's name; Riblah was the trial of that broken oath.
b: The Hebrew is literally "he spoke judgments with him," the language of a court, and the Plain English Translation uses the wording of Jeremiah 52:9, where the Hebrew is the same (2 Kings 25:6 has a different noun, "his case was judged"). Ezekiel says what the charge was: Zedekiah had sworn an oath of loyalty by God's name and then sent to Egypt for horses (Ezekiel 17:11–21), and Chronicles says the same: "Against King Nebuchadnezzar, too, he rebelled, though Nebuchadnezzar had put him under oath by God" (2 Chronicles 36:13). The punishment was a treaty-breaker's. Riblah, on the Orontes in Syria, was the Babylonian army's headquarters in these years, as it had been Pharaoh Neco's after Josiah's death (2 Kings 23:33).

a: all the nobles of Judah
p: The three tellings of the fall share most of their words and differ in a few places that matter.
b: Jeremiah 39:4–10 runs close to 2 Kings 25:4–12 and Jeremiah 52:7–16, and the Plain English Translation uses the same English where the Hebrew is the same (for example "went after", "hauled up", "gate between the double walls", "bronze fetters"). The differences: 39:6 says the king of Babylon killed "the nobles of Judah" (chorim); Jeremiah 52:10 has "the officials of Judah" (sarim) at Riblah; 2 Kings 25:7 does not mention them there (2 Kings 25:18–21 tells of officials put to death at Riblah). 39:7 stops at the fetters; Jeremiah 52:11 adds the house of punishment until his death. 39:8 names the king's house and "the house of the people" and the walls, but not the Temple (2 Kings 25:9; Jeremiah 52:13). 39:3 and the verses after give no day for the burning; 2 Kings 25:8 says the seventh day and Jeremiah 52:12 the tenth. 39:9 has the rest of the people "who had gone over"; Jeremiah 52:15 begins with a further group, "some of the poor of the people". 39:10 says Nebuzaradan "gave them vineyards and fields"; 2 Kings 25:12 and Jeremiah 52:16 have nearly the same Hebrew words, but there they are workers, "to tend vines and to plow".

a: Zedekiah's eyes he put out
t: Two prophecies that both came true
p: Jeremiah said Zedekiah would see the king of Babylon face to face; Ezekiel said he would not see Babylon.
b: Zedekiah's blinding fits two messages that sounded opposed. Jeremiah told him he would meet the king of Babylon face to face (Jeremiah 34:3); Ezekiel said he would be brought to Babylon but would not see it (Ezekiel 12:13). The last thing Zedekiah saw was Nebuchadnezzar at Riblah and his own sons' deaths (39:6); then he was blinded and taken to Babylon. Jewish tradition and many Christian commentators read this as the standard example of two true prophecies that look contradictory until the event. Jeremiah 34:4–5 also promised he would "die in peace", a promise that depended on his obeying; Jeremiah 52:11 says he stayed in prison until he died.

a: The king's house and the house of the people
p: This verse names the palace and the houses but not the Temple. Other tellings name it.
b: Jeremiah 39 leaves out the burning of the Temple. 2 Kings 25:9 says "He set the LORD's house on fire" and Jeremiah 52:13 says the same. Commentators take the omission in different ways: this chapter is a short summary written to introduce Jeremiah's own fate; the Temple's fall is told elsewhere in the book; or the chapter was cut down by a scribe who knew chapter 52. The Greek has none of 39:4–13, so the question does not arise in that edition. The Hebrew has "the house of the king and the house of the people," with "house" in the singular; the Plain English Translation keeps the singular. It may mean the people's houses taken together (compare "all the houses of Jerusalem" in 2 Kings 25:9) or a public building; the Hebrew does not say. Yigal Shiloh's excavations in the City of David (1978–1985) found burned houses with ash and arrowheads from the Babylonian destruction. The Temple Mount has not been excavated.

a: the poor ones who had nothing at all
t: A land that was not empty
p: The poor were left to farm. Archaeology shows Judah was badly hurt, but not emptied.
b: Babylon's habit was to take the skilled and leave the poor to work the land, and the new owners of "vineyards and fields" are here named (see also 2 Kings 25:12; Jeremiah 52:16). Scholars disagree on how many were left. Hans Barstad argued from the evidence that the land was never "empty" in the exile and that life went on in much of Judah. Oded Lipschits finds Jerusalem and the hill country around it greatly reduced in the sixth century, while the district of Benjamin to the north, where Mizpah and Gibeon lay, kept its population and became the center of the province. Both agree that the people of the land who stayed are the ones Jeremiah 40:6–12 calls the remnant.

a: watch over him
p: The Hebrew says 'set your eyes on him', a phrase of care, which Jeremiah uses of God himself.
b: "Set your eyes on him" is a Hebrew idiom for taking someone under your protection, not for watching him. The same phrase describes God's care for the exiles of 597: "I will set my eyes on them for good" (Jeremiah 24:6); and Nebuzaradan says it of himself in 40:4. In the Hebrew a written word, 'im ("except"), stands before "as he says to you" but is not read aloud (a Ketiv without a Qere); the meaning is "do only what he says."
orig: שִׂים עֵינֶיךָ עָלָיו (sim 'einekha 'alav), 'set your eyes on him'

a: Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan
p: Gedaliah came from the family of scribes who had served Josiah and who stood by Jeremiah.
b: Gedaliah's grandfather Shaphan was King Josiah's secretary who read the newly found law book to the king (2 Kings 22:3–10). His father Ahikam saved Jeremiah from execution (Jeremiah 26:24), and his uncles and cousins appear on Jeremiah's side or close to the court: Gemariah in whose room Baruch read the scroll (36:10–12), and Elasah who carried Jeremiah's letter to Babylon (29:3). A clay seal impression from Lachish reads "belonging to Gedaliah, who is over the house," found in a burned layer from this period in 1935. It is widely thought to be this man, from the time before he was governor, when he held the royal steward's office; the identification is probable but not certain, since the name was common.

a: Ebed-melech the Cushite
t: The foreigner who is promised his life
p: Ebed-melech rescued Jeremiah from the cistern (38:7–13) and now gets a promise of his own.
b: The name means "the king's servant," and it may be a title more than a personal name. He was a Cushite (from Nubia, south of Egypt), a court official (38:7 gives him that rank; here the text says only "the Cushite") who spoke up for Jeremiah against the princes. The words are placed after the fall, but the chapter says they had come to Jeremiah earlier, while he was still shut up in the courtyard of the guard. They set a foreigner who trusted God against Zedekiah, the king of Judah, who feared men (38:19) and lost his sons and his eyes.

a: Your life will be yours as loot
p: A soldier who loses everything but escapes alive carries off his life as his only loot. Jeremiah says it four times.
b: The idiom comes from war: the winner takes plunder, the loser who gets away alive takes his own life as loot. Jeremiah first uses it as advice to the people: surrender to Babylon and your life will be your loot (21:9; 38:2). It is a promise made to a person only twice more, and each time to someone who is not a king or a prince: to Ebed-melech here, "because you trusted in me," and to Baruch (45:5). "Trusted" is the word Jeremiah uses for the opposite of trusting in people (17:5–8).

a: sent him away from Ramah
p: Jeremiah is freed in 39:11–14 and again here. Readers explain it in three ways.
b: In 39:14 Jeremiah goes to Gedaliah's care straight from the prison courtyard; here he is found in chains in the exiles' camp at Ramah. One release, told twice: the two passages are two accounts of the same event that were joined, and the Greek's lack of 39:4–13 leaves them closer together. Two stages: he was released to Gedaliah (39:14), and then, when Gedaliah's staff was gathered with the captives, caught up by mistake in the roundup and freed again at Ramah. A summary and its detail: 39:14 gives the outcome and 40:1–6 the story behind it. The commentaries listed here discuss these options.

a: Ramah
p: Jeremiah 31:15 puts Rachel weeping at Ramah. This is the one story that puts the exiles there.
b: Ramah (modern er-Ram, about five miles north of Jerusalem in Benjamin) was a gathering point on the road north. Jeremiah 31:15, which puts Rachel's weeping at Ramah, is linked by some readers to this scene, where the exiles of Jerusalem and Judah stand chained and Jeremiah himself is among them. Matthew quotes that verse for the children of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:17–18). Whether 31:15 had Ramah's captives in mind or only the ancient tomb of Rachel (Genesis 35:19–20; 1 Samuel 10:2) is argued; see the notes at 31:15.

a: The LORD your God announced this calamity for this place
t: A Babylonian who speaks like a prophet
p: A foreign officer explains the fall in Jeremiah's own terms. Why?
b: Nebuzaradan says the LORD, "your God," brought the disaster because of Judah's sin and disobedience, the verdict of the book's prose sermons. Some readers take him at his word: he had heard Jeremiah's preaching or had been told to treat the prophet kindly (39:11–12), and a victor can say that a conquered people's god had handed them over. Others, such as McKane and Carroll, say the book's authors are putting their own theology into a foreigner's mouth. The Rabshakeh of Assyria also speaks as if the LORD sent him (2 Kings 18:25), which shows that such speeches were part of how these stories were told. The effect is the same: even the enemy agrees the fall was God's judgment and not his defeat.

a: While Jeremiah was still not turning around
t: A hard clause, and a word for turning
p: The clause is hard. The Plain English Translation keeps 'turn' in both halves; Swete's Greek reads 'And if not, go back to Gedaliah.'
b: The Hebrew we'odenu lo yashuv weshuvah is hard: literally "and while he was still not returning, and return!" The Plain English Translation keeps both forms of the verb shuv, "turn back," so the English reader sees the word that Jeremiah uses elsewhere for turning away from God or back to him (3:12–14; 8:4–5), here used for ordinary movement: Nebuzaradan's "Go back" is about place, not repentance. One way to read the first clause is that Jeremiah had not yet turned to leave when the officer added his advice. The clause may also be damaged. Swete's Greek reads "and if not, go back" (Greek 47:5, with an added "run off"), which turns it into a further offer: if he does not want Babylon, he should go to Gedaliah. Either way, Jeremiah is given the choice and takes Gedaliah. See the variant.

a: Mizpah
p: With Jerusalem in ruins, Mizpah became the center of what was left of Judah.
b: Mizpah is usually placed at Tell en-Nasbeh, about eight miles north of Jerusalem, dug by William Badè from 1926 to 1935. Some prefer Nebi Samwil. Tell en-Nasbeh shows no burned layer for 586 BC and had a strong sixth-century settlement, which fits a choice of Mizpah by Babylon over the burned capital; Oded Lipschits and Jeffrey Zorn argue that it was the seat of the province for a time. King Asa had walled it against Baasha (1 Kings 15:22). No Babylonian text calls Gedaliah "governor"; the Hebrew says only that he was "put in charge" (40:5, 7), as the site's 2 Kings 25:22 does.

a: Johanan and Jonathan the sons of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth, the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, and Jezaniah son of the Maacathite
p: These are the guerrilla captains who held out in the hills. A seal from Mizpah may name one.
b: The commanders had escaped the siege and fought on in the open country (compare 2 Kings 25:4–5). 2 Kings 25:23 lists four of the names, with Jaazaniah for Jezaniah (two forms of one name). A stamp seal from Tell en-Nasbeh reads "belonging to Jaazaniah, servant of the king," with a fighting rooster; it dates to the late monarchy and is often linked to this commander, though the name was common. The written (Ketiv) form of "Ephai" is "Ophai" and the Plain English Translation follows the spoken (Qere) form; see the variant.

a: stand before the Chaldeans
p: Gedaliah says he will represent them to the Babylonian officials who visit.
b: To "stand before" someone is to serve or speak for others in front of a ruler. It is what a prophet or priest does before God (Jeremiah 15:1, 19) and what Gedaliah promises here: he will meet each Babylonian inspector and answer for the people. The commanders' part is to farm. Wine, summer fruit (probably dried figs and other tree fruit picked at the end of summer) and oil are the three crops of Judah's hills.

a: Judeans
p: The Hebrew is Yehudim. It means people of Judah, and in Jeremiah it is becoming the word for the Jews.
b: Yehudim appears in the Bible first in 2 Kings (16:6; 25:25) and then in Jeremiah (32:12; 34:9; 38:19; 40:11–12; 41:3; 43:9; 44:1; 52:28, 30). Here it is still a geographic name: people from Judah. The Plain English Translation says "Judeans" to keep that sense. Later Hebrew, Greek Ioudaioi and English "Jews" grew out of this word, once the people of Judah were scattered across the Babylonian, Egyptian and Persian worlds and carried the name with them.

a: Baalis king of the Ammonites
p: A clay seal impression from Tell el-Umeiri in Jordan may carry this king's name.
b: Ammon, east of the Jordan, had stayed free of Babylon longer than Judah; Zedekiah's rebels had sought its help (Jeremiah 27:3). It also sheltered Judean refugees (40:11). In 1984 the excavators at Tell el-Umeiri found a seal impression reading "belonging to Milkom'ur, servant of Ba'alyasha'," a name that many scholars identify with Baalis. The identification is likely but not proved; the Hebrew spelling here and the Greek ("Beleisa") differ slightly. Why Baalis wanted Gedaliah dead is not told. A Babylonian governor on his western border, using Mizpah as a base, would have been a threat to Ammon.

a: let me go and strike down Ishmael son of Nethaniah
p: Johanan's offer to kill Ishmael secretly looks like prudence. Gedaliah thought it was slander.
b: Readers judge Gedaliah differently. Some readers see a good man whose trust in people made him blind to danger, and the Talmud holds that his death weighs as heavily as the Temple's burning (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 18b). Others point out that a governor who was Babylon's appointee could not allow his own officers to murder a royal prince on a rumor, and that Johanan, who later led the people to Egypt, was not always a wise judge of risk. Johanan's argument was that the whole remnant was at stake (40:15), and events proved him right on the facts.

a: In the seventh month
p: The text does not say. The seventh month came just after the fall by one count, and years later by another.
b: The simplest reading puts the murder in the autumn of 586, a few weeks after the temple burned. Some scholars find too much happening in two months (harvest, a sizable return of refugees, Ammon's plot) and place the murder later. They link it to Jeremiah 52:30, which says Nebuzaradan deported 745 Judeans in Nebuchadnezzar's twenty-third year (582/581 BC) and could be Babylon's answer to the killing. Josephus puts Nebuchadnezzar's Egyptian campaign in the twenty-third year as well (Antiquities 10.180-182 (10.9.7 in Whiston's numbering)), but his account is late and not independent, and it does not say that Jeremiah or Baruch was among the captives he took to Babylon. Jewish tradition keeps the fast of Gedaliah on the third of Tishri, the day after the New Year (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 18b).

a: There at Mizpah they ate a meal together.
t: Eating bread with the man you will kill
p: Ishmael's murder happens at a shared meal, which in the Bible is a pledge of peace.
b: Eating bread together was a sign of friendship and a covenant of safety (Genesis 31:54; Exodus 18:12). Betrayal at the table is a sorrow in Scripture: In Psalm 41:9 a close friend who ate the poet's bread turns on him, and Jesus applies the verse to Judas (John 13:18). Ishmael came with ten men as guests of the man he was about to kill, and he spent a day acting as if nothing had happened (41:4-6).

a: one of the royal line
p: 2 Kings tells the same story in five verses. Jeremiah adds most of the detail.
b: 2 Kings 25:22–26 is a short version of the story told in Jeremiah 40–41. Where the Hebrew is the same the Plain English Translation uses the same English ("put in charge", "one of the royal line", Ishmael's ten men). The differences: 40:8 names more commanders than 2 Kings 25:23 (it adds Jonathan and the sons of Ephai), and spells Jezaniah where 2 Kings has Jaazaniah. 40:9 has Gedaliah say "you have nothing to fear from serving the Chaldeans"; 2 Kings 25:24 has "Don't fear the Chaldeans' servants" (see the variant). 41:1 adds "the king's chief men" and the meal; 2 Kings has neither. 2 Kings does not tell of Jeremiah (40:1–6), the harvest (40:10–12), Johanan's warning (40:13–16), the eighty mourners and the cistern (41:4–9), Ishmael's captives and Johanan's pursuit (41:10–16), or the stop at Geruth Kimham (41:17). It has the murder and the flight to Egypt in a few lines (2 Kings 25:25–26), and it does not name Jeremiah.

a: had cut themselves
p: Eighty men from the old northern kingdom came to the ruined Temple, with the signs of grief.
b: Shaved beards, torn clothes and gashed skin were the marks of mourning. The Law forbade the cutting (Leviticus 19:28; Deuteronomy 14:1), but it was done in Jeremiah's time (16:6; 47:5; 48:37). The men came from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria, towns that had belonged to the northern kingdom taken by Assyria 130 years earlier, to bring grain offerings and frankincense "to the house of the LORD." So after 586 the site was still treated as holy, and some form of altar worship probably went on among the ruins. Swete's Greek names "Salem" for Shiloh.
r: Leviticus 19:28; Deuteronomy 14:1; Jeremiah 16:6; Jeremiah 48:37; Zechariah 7:3; Lamentations 2:6–7

a: We have hidden stores in the field
p: Ten men bought their lives with a hoard of wheat, barley, oil and honey.
b: Storing food in underground pits, jars or caves was common in Judah. Honey in the Bible can be bees' honey or fruit syrup. The scene shows how scarce food was after the siege and why 40:12 stresses an "abundance" of wine and fruit.

a: beside Gedaliah
p: The Hebrew says 'by the hand of Gedaliah'. Four guesses are possible.
b: The Hebrew reads "the corpses of the men he had struck down beyad Gedalyahu," literally "by the hand of Gedaliah." Proposed senses: beside Gedaliah, that is, with his body (the Plain English Translation); because of Gedaliah, as the King James Version has it; on account of the arrangement Gedaliah had made; or an error (the Greek has no such phrase). In every reading the cistern was full of the dead. See the variant.

a: King Asa had made because of Baasha king of Israel
p: Asa fortified Mizpah in the war with Baasha. Tell en-Nasbeh has large rock-cut cisterns.
b: 1 Kings 15:22 says Asa used the stones Baasha had left at Ramah to build up Geba and Mizpah; 2 Chronicles 16:6 says the same. The excavators of Tell en-Nasbeh found large water cisterns cut into the rock, but none has been tied to this story. Swete's Greek calls it "a great cistern" (Greek 48:9); the Hebrew has no "great" and the Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew (see the variant). Ishmael's mass grave is the grim ending of that old defense.

a: by the great waters at Gibeon
p: An enormous rock-cut pool at el-Jib has been dug. The same place made wine.
b: James Pritchard dug at el-Jib, the site of Gibeon, from 1956 to 1962. He found a round pool cut into the rock, about eleven meters across and about as deep, with a staircase winding down to the water table (compare 2 Samuel 2:13, "the pool of Gibeon"). He also found a seventh-century wine-making installation, rock-cut cellars for storing jars, and jar handles stamped "Gibeon" with the owners' names. That fits Jeremiah 40:10–12, where the people were told to gather wine, and shows why Ishmael's captives were camped in Gibeon's neighborhood.

a: Kimham
p: The place name means 'the lodging of Chimham', after Barzillai's son.
b: Geruth is related to gur, to stay as a foreigner, and means a lodging place or inn. Chimham was the son of Barzillai the Gileadite, whom David took to Jerusalem as a reward (2 Samuel 19:37–40; 1 Kings 2:7). The lodging place near Bethlehem is usually thought to preserve his name and a grant David made him, though the books of Samuel and Kings do not say so. The written form (Ketiv) is a different word, kemohem, "like them," and the Plain English Translation follows the spoken form (Qere). The place lay on the road south from Bethlehem to Hebron and Egypt.

a: pray for us to the LORD your God
t: The prayer Jeremiah was told not to pray
p: Earlier the LORD forbade Jeremiah to pray for this people. Now they ask, and he agrees.
b: Four times in the first half of the book the LORD tells Jeremiah not to pray for the people (7:16; 11:14; 14:11; 15:1; compare 18:20). Now the survivors ask for exactly that, and the prophet promises to do it (42:4). No ban is repeated: the sentence has been carried out, and what is left of Judah is a small group who can be addressed again. Jeremiah's role as an intercessor, in the line of Moses and Samuel (15:1), is what they ask him to be.
r: Jeremiah 7:16; Jeremiah 11:14; Jeremiah 14:11; Jeremiah 15:1; Exodus 32:11–14; 1 Samuel 12:23

a: After ten days
p: Jeremiah's answer takes ten days. A true word could not be ordered on demand.
b: False prophets in Jeremiah always have a word ready (23:25–32; 28:1–4). Jeremiah waits ten days for the LORD, and the delay is part of how the story shows his word to be genuine. The people had asked for an answer at once and promised to obey it whatever it was (42:5–6). A fragment of 2QJer preserves "ten days" and the rest of 42:7 as they stand in the Hebrew text (its first two words are restored).

a: I will build you up and not demolish you. I will plant you and not pull you up.
p: These four verbs come from Jeremiah's call, here with the promise side first.
b: At his call Jeremiah was set over nations "to pull up and pull down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant" (1:10). Four of those six verbs return here: build (banah), demolish (haras), plant (nata) and pull up (natash). The Plain English Translation gives each the same English wherever the four recur in this form (1:10; 24:6; 42:10; 45:4). The same Hebrew verbs appear in the LORD's rule for dealing with a nation, which he can reverse (18:7–10), and in the promise that he will watch over Israel to build and to plant as he once watched to tear down (31:28). The offer here is that the remnant can still be the plant and the building. In 45:4 the verbs run the other way.

a: I have changed my mind about the harm I have done to you
p: The Hebrew nicham can mean sorrow, a change of course or comfort. The Plain English Translation says the LORD 'changes his mind'.
b: Nicham (Niphal) covers grief, regret and a change of mind. When the LORD is its subject in Jeremiah the Plain English Translation says he changes his mind about the harm he planned (26:3, 13, 19; 15:6, "I am tired of changing my mind"), the rule laid down in 18:7–10. Here the harm is the destruction he has already brought, and the verse says he has turned from it: if the remnant stays, he will build and not demolish. Some translate "I am sorry for the harm I have done," and that shade of the word is in the Hebrew too. The Greek has "I have been eased over the evils I did to you" (Greek 49:10, anapepaumai), taking the verb in its sense of comfort. Samuel can say that God does not change his mind as a human being does (1 Samuel 15:29) while the same chapter says he was sorry he had made Saul king (1 Samuel 15:11); see the topic on God's regret. 2QJer has the same words here, with spelling differences only.
r: Jeremiah 18:7–10; Jeremiah 26:3; Jeremiah 26:13; 1 Samuel 15:11; 1 Samuel 15:29; Exodus 32:14

a: we will go into the land of Egypt
p: Going back to Egypt was the covenant's last curse, and Israel's oldest warning.
b: The people dream of a land with no war, no ram's horn alarms and no hunger, the opposite of the siege. But the Law ended its list of curses with a return to Egypt: the LORD would take them back to Egypt in ships (Deuteronomy 28:68), and the king was never to send people back there for horses (Deuteronomy 17:16). Hosea said the same: "they will return to Egypt" (Hosea 8:13; 9:3; 11:5). Isaiah warned against going down to Egypt for help (Isaiah 30:1–5; 31:1). For Jeremiah's hearers this was not only unwise; it would undo the Exodus.
r: Deuteronomy 28:68; Deuteronomy 17:16; Hosea 8:13; Hosea 9:3; Hosea 11:5; Isaiah 30:1–5; Isaiah 31:1

a: by famine and by disease
p: Jeremiah's stock triple. The Greek often keeps only two.
b: The Hebrew herev, ra'av, deber is Jeremiah's favorite way to speak of a siege: it appears over a dozen times (14:12; 21:7, 9; 24:10; 27:8, 13; 29:17–18; 32:24, 36; 34:17; 38:2; and in 42:17, 22; 44:13). Deber means an epidemic and is the Plain English Translation's "disease" in every case. In chapters 42 and 44 the Greek has only "sword and famine" and lacks "disease"; at 44:13 2QJer has the word and so agrees with the Hebrew text. See the variants.
r: Jeremiah 14:12; Jeremiah 21:7; Jeremiah 24:10; Jeremiah 27:8; Jeremiah 29:17; Jeremiah 44:13; Ezekiel 5:12

a: a curse, a horror, a word used in cursing and a disgrace
t: Four words for a ruined people
p: Only 42:18 and 44:12 carry this exact list of four. A 'curse word' is a name people say in curses.
b: The Hebrew is 'alah, shammah, qelalah, cherpah. Qelalah is the word used in cursing: "May the LORD make you like ..." (compare the curse the exiles in Babylon will use, 29:22). The words describe not only suffering but being made a warning for others to point at. All four appear together only at 42:18 and 44:12, where the pattern is aimed at Judeans in Egypt. Other passages use related lists with different members: 24:9 (terror, evil, disgrace, byword, taunt, curse), 25:18 (ruin, horror, hissing, curse), 29:18 (horror, curse, shock, hissing, disgrace), and 44:8 has only curse and disgrace. The promise of 42:18 offers to people who leave the same fate Jerusalem got.
r: Jeremiah 24:9; Jeremiah 25:18; Jeremiah 29:18; Jeremiah 29:22; Jeremiah 44:8; Jeremiah 44:12

a: You have led your own lives astray
t: A word written one way and read another
p: The written text says 'I led you astray'; the reading tradition says 'you led yourselves astray'.
b: The word is written one way and read another. The written form (Ketiv) is analyzed in the Leningrad text as a first-person verb with a plural object ending, hit'etei-m, "I led you astray." The vowels in the Codex belong to hit'item, "you led astray," which with "in your lives" gives the Qere, "you led your own lives astray." The Plain English Translation follows the Qere. The written form would make Jeremiah say he misled them with the oracle they asked for, which fits poorly with "for you sent me" in the next clause. Swete's Greek has "you did wrong against your own lives" (Greek 49:20), which shares the Qere's sense and puts the fault on the people. 2QJer breaks off before this verse. See the variant.

a: You are speaking a lie!
t: Calling the true prophet a liar
p: The same charge Jeremiah made against the false prophets is aimed back at him.
b: "Sheqer" (lie) is Jeremiah's word for the false prophets' work (5:31; 14:14; 23:25–26; 27:10, 14–16; 29:21). Here it is shouted at Jeremiah by Azariah, Johanan and "the arrogant men" (the zedim, an ugly word for proud defiance). Hananiah's challenge in chapter 28 was the same kind of quarrel. The test the Law gave for a prophet, that his word comes true (Deuteronomy 18:21–22), could not be used on the spot: the people did not wait for the evidence. Swete's Greek reads "Azariah son of Maaseiah" here and at 42:1, where the Hebrew has "Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah"; see the variants.

a: Baruch son of Neriah is turning you against us
p: The accusation shows how Baruch was seen: as the scribe with influence over the prophet.
b: Baruch had written down Jeremiah's words (Jeremiah 36) and belonged to a family of officials (his brother Seraiah, 51:59). The charge is that the scribe is the real author of Jeremiah's advice to stay, and that he wants the people handed to the Chaldeans. There is no hint that this was true. It is the reply of people who cannot bear the message and look for an explanation in the messenger's circle. Baruch is named again in 45, where Jeremiah gives him a message of his own. Later books were put under his name (Baruch, 2 Baruch and others); see the topic on Baruch for who counts which as Scripture.

a: Nebuzaradan the chief of the guard had left with Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan
p: The group that goes to Egypt includes the king's daughters, Jeremiah and Baruch.
b: Everyone Gedaliah had been given charge of now goes, willing or not, including the "king's daughters," the princesses entrusted to him (41:10). Jeremiah and Baruch go too, "taken" by the commanders and not choosing it. This is the point at which Jeremiah leaves the land he was told to build and plant. The Lives of the Prophets, short Jewish accounts of the prophets from about the first century AD that survive in Christian copies, say he was stoned to death by his own people in Egypt; the tradition appears nowhere in Jeremiah and cannot be checked. Josephus also has Johanan carry Jeremiah and Baruch to Egypt (Antiquities 10.9.6 in Whiston's numbering); the passage on Nebuchadnezzar's later attack on Egypt (Antiquities 10.180-182 (10.9.7 in Whiston's numbering)) speaks of captives taken to Babylon but does not name Jeremiah or Baruch among them. See the variant for how 4QJer-d and the Greek read this verse.

a: Tahpanhes
p: Tell Defenneh, in the Egyptian Delta, was the first stop for anyone coming from Judah.
b: Tahpanhes (Greek Daphnae, modern Tell Defenneh) was a fortress on the eastern frontier built in the 600s BC to guard the road from Asia; Herodotus mentions its garrison (Histories 2.30) and names the place (2.107). In 1886 Flinders Petrie dug there. He found a large fortified mudbrick building, which the local people called Qasr Bint el-Yahudi, "the palace of the Jew's daughter," and he identified a brick platform near its entrance as the one Jeremiah means (43:9). Later archaeologists doubt that the platform is Pharaoh's house or the stone-burying place. Tahpanhes is also named in Jeremiah 2:16, Ezekiel 30:18 and Jeremiah 46:14.

a: mortar of the brick terrace
t: A brick terrace, a kiln or mortar?
p: The Hebrew malben is a rare word; versions take it as 'brick-kiln', 'pavement' or 'terrace'.
b: Malben is related to levenah, "brick." The King James Version has "brickkiln"; many modern versions take it as a pavement or platform of brick; the Greek omits it and has the stones hidden in "the gateways" of Pharaoh's house. "Mortar" translates melet, which can mean mortar or clay. The picture is a flat brickwork surface in front of the palace gate, with the stones set into its clay. See the variant for the reading of 4QJer-d.

a: my servant
p: The LORD calls the king who burned the Temple his servant. The Greek and some scholars find that hard.
b: The Hebrew 'avdi, "my servant," is the title of Moses, David and the prophets, here given to a pagan king as the instrument of God's plan (25:9; 27:6; 43:10). It does not praise him; Babylon's own end is foretold in chapters 50–51. The Greek lacks "my servant" at all three places, and some scholars think it was added to the Hebrew text in a later edition, while others think the Greek dropped it because it troubled readers. 2QJer has the word here, so the Hebrew text with that title was already in circulation by the time of the Dead Sea Scrolls.

a: He will come and strike the land of Egypt.
p: No Babylonian text says he took Egypt. A fragment shows a campaign in 568/567 BC.
b: Ezekiel also foretold Nebuchadnezzar's march on Egypt and dated one oracle to 571 BC (Ezekiel 29:17–20). A Babylonian fragment (British Museum 33041) records that in his thirty-seventh year (568/567) he marched against Egypt and that King Amasis called out his army, but the damaged text does not say what happened. Josephus says Nebuchadnezzar attacked Egypt in the twenty-third year, killed its king, set up another and took the Jews there captive to Babylon (Antiquities 10.180-182 (10.9.7 in Whiston's numbering)); no earlier source supports it, and he does not name Jeremiah or Baruch among the captives. Readers take the facts in three ways: the prophecy was partly fulfilled by the 568/567 raid; it was a forecast not met in detail, as a prophet's image of judgment; or its larger sense was met in Persia's conquest of Egypt in 525 BC. Egyptian sources show no Babylonian rule. See 46:13–26 and the topic on Egypt.

a: pick the land of Egypt clean, as a shepherd picks his cloak clean of lice
p: The Hebrew verb can mean 'wrap himself in' or, as the Greek reads it, 'pick clean of lice'.
b: The verb 'atah usually means "wrap oneself in," and the King James Version has "array himself." The Greek reads phtheirizo, "delouse," and some lexicons give a second root of that meaning. The Plain English Translation follows the delousing sense, which also suits the shepherd's quick work and his leaving "in peace." Either way the picture is of ease: a shepherd deals with his cloak without a struggle, and the king will take Egypt the same way. The Greek has "Heliopolis" for Beth-shemesh in the next verse.

a: standing stones of Beth-shemesh
p: This Beth-shemesh is 'house of the sun', the city the Egyptians called Iunu and the Bible On.
b: Heliopolis, the "city of the sun," northeast of modern Cairo, was the center of the sun-god Re. Joseph married the daughter of its priest (Genesis 41:45). Its great stone pillars were obelisks, and the Greek translates them with the word for pillars (stuloi). The Egyptian obelisks now in London, Paris and New York came from there. Isaiah 19:18 speaks of "the City of the Sun" in a prophecy that Egypt will one day turn to the LORD. In both the Hebrew "standing stones" of Egypt and the idols of Canaan are the kind the Law bans.

a: Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis and the land of Pathros
p: The refugees spread from the Delta fortresses to Upper Egypt. A later Judean garrison at Elephantine is known from its own papyri.
b: Migdol (Magdolos) and Tahpanhes were frontier forts in the northeast Delta; Memphis (Hebrew Noph) was the old capital; Pathros is Upper Egypt, from the Egyptian "southern land" (Isaiah 11:11; Ezekiel 29:14; 30:14). Beyond this chapter our evidence comes from Elephantine, an island at the first cataract, where Judeans served as soldiers in the Persian period. Their papyri (about 495–399 BC) show a temple to "YHW" there which they say had stood since "the days of the kings of Egypt," before Cambyses came in 525 BC. Whether the community began with these refugees or earlier is not known. The Greek lacks "Memphis"; see the variant.

a: rising early
t: My servants the prophets, early and often
p: A phrase used again and again in the book for the prophets God kept sending.
b: "Rising early and sending" pictures a master who gets up at dawn to send his messengers. It appears in 7:25; 25:4; 26:5; 29:19; 32:33; 35:14–15 and here, and is a mark of the prose sermons that scholars link with Deuteronomy's style (Thiel, Nicholson). Whether Jeremiah's own words or his editors', it gathers the whole prophetic line, Moses to Jeremiah, into one long appeal that the people refused. The phrase gods they did not know (44:3) comes from Deuteronomy 32:17 and 13:6.
r: Jeremiah 7:25; Jeremiah 25:4; Jeremiah 26:5; Jeremiah 35:15; 2 Kings 17:13; Deuteronomy 32:17

a: the evil deeds of the kings of Judah and of their wives
p: Queen mothers and royal wives led worship in Judah. Maacah and Athaliah are the examples.
b: "Their wives" probably points at queens and queen mothers who shaped the cult at court: Maacah set up an image of Asherah, and Asa removed her as queen mother (1 Kings 15:13); Athaliah brought Baal worship from the north (2 Kings 11:18). In the Hebrew a queen mother, gevirah, held an office of her own. The Greek reads "your rulers" in this list instead; see the variant.
r: 1 Kings 15:13; 2 Kings 11:18; 2 Kings 21:7; 2 Kings 23:4–7; Jeremiah 13:18; Jeremiah 29:2

a: all the women standing there in a great crowd
p: Men and women answer together, but the women lead. The speech sets out a rival reading of history.
b: The men "knew" their wives were burning incense; the women stood by in a great crowd, and the word that follows is a joint reply. Women kept the household cult in Judah (Jeremiah 7:18 shows the whole family at work; Ezekiel 8:14 has women weeping for Tammuz). The women's speech is neither a defense of an unfamiliar cult nor a confession; it is a claim about cause and effect that Jeremiah answers with his own (44:21–23). Susan Ackerman reads it as the voice of popular religion in sixth-century Judah, where women's offerings were part of ordinary life. Others read it as plain defiance of the prophet. The Hebrew uses masculine nouns for the "people" but feminine verbs in 44:25.

a: the Queen of Heaven
t: Who was the Queen of Heaven?
p: A goddess tied to Ishtar and Astarte, worshiped with incense, drink offerings and cakes. Her exact name is not known.
b: "Queen of Heaven" (melekhet hashamayim; the Greek has basilissa tou ouranou) is not a name but a title. In Mesopotamia Ishtar was "queen of heaven" (sharrat shame), and her West Semitic cousin Astarte was close to her in character. Egypt had Isis and Hathor, whom Egyptian texts also call "lady of heaven." Many scholars take the goddess of Jeremiah to be Ishtar-Astarte as worshiped in Judah, since Jeremiah 7:18 says the whole family joined in the cult before the exile, and the many hundreds of clay "pillar figurines" of a female figure found in Judean homes (Raz Kletter) fit that picture; others suggest Asherah or Anat. Inscriptions at Kuntillet Ajrud ("Yahweh of Samaria and his asherah") and the Aramaic papyri of Elephantine, where oaths are sworn by "Anat-Yahu," show that female deities were honored beside the LORD in Judean communities. How far that was Israelite religion and how far a deviation is argued: Mark Smith and William Dever see it as part of ordinary religion; Jeremiah and the Deuteronomists call it idolatry. See also the note at 7:18.

a: just as we did, we and our ancestors, our kings and our officials
p: The women say the kings and officials had done the same. The books of Kings agree that foreign cults were common.
b: The speakers describe the worship as the religion of the whole realm, kings and officials included, and the books of Kings agree that for much of the monarchy foreign cults stood in Jerusalem (2 Kings 21:1–7; 23:4–14). Jeremiah never denies that it was widespread. Where he and the women differ is the meaning of the facts: they read prosperity as the gods' reward; he reads the fall as the LORD's reckoning for the same acts (44:21–23). The question of how much of Judah's religion was plural before the exile is one of the most argued in Old Testament study.

a: from the time we quit burning incense
p: The women date their troubles to when the offerings ceased. Which stopping do they mean?
b: The women's argument has a time-line: plenty before, disaster since. Josiah's reform (about 622 BC) is the usual answer: Josiah purged the high places and the Asherah from the temple (2 Kings 23:4–7), and then died at Megiddo in 609, and Judah's fortunes fell. The last years is the second: Zedekiah's reforms and the siege, when the cult was supposed to have been cut off (compare Jeremiah 34:8–10). The third is simply the exile's days of want. Commentators often favor Josiah's reform, since the women remember a time of plenty before it.

a: is it without our husbands
p: Under the Law a husband could cancel a wife's vow. The women say theirs did not.
b: Numbers 30:6–15 gives the husband the right to annul his wife's vow on the day he hears of it; if he says nothing, the vow stands. This law is probably behind the women's question: the men knew (44:15) and said nothing, so the vows are valid. Jeremiah's answer in 44:25 is that this makes them legally binding and no less wrong.

a: cakes
p: The Hebrew kavvanim is a loan word. Babylonian ritual texts have a similar cake for Ishtar.
b: Kavvanim is found only here and in Jeremiah 7:18. The Akkadian kamanu names a kind of cake offered to Ishtar, and the Hebrew is widely taken to be its borrowing. Radak takes the word to mean foods prepared and presented to the Queen of Heaven. The verb "to shape her image" (leha'atsivah) is rare and may mean molding the cake in her form or, as some think, "to give her pain" (the root 'atsav means both to shape and to hurt). The Greek omits the phrase altogether.

a: Did it not come into his mind?
p: 'Come up on his heart' is Hebrew for 'to think of'. It sets God's memory against the women's claim.
b: The Hebrew 'alah 'al lev, "to come up on the heart," means to think of or remember (Jeremiah 3:16; 7:31; 19:5; 32:35). Here the LORD's memory is an indictment: the incense the women count as part of their own prosperity is what the LORD "remembered." "Remember" in the Bible is the language of covenant, and it can go either way (Genesis 8:1; Exodus 2:24; Psalm 25:7).

a: Very well! Make your vows stand. Carry out your vows!
p: The command is bitter irony, and the verbs show the women were the speakers.
b: Jeremiah uses the strong double forms of the original: "establish, establish your vows; perform, perform them." He is mocking, not ordering. The verbs "have spoken" and "carried out" are feminine plural in Hebrew, though the opening words are masculine ("you and your wives"). It is the women's vows that are in view. The Greek reads "You women ..." without "you and your wives." See the variant.

a: As the Lord GOD lives
t: The oath that will not be sworn
p: Judeans swore 'As the LORD lives'. The LORD takes that oath from their mouths in Egypt.
b: To swear "As the LORD lives" was to use the name of the God of Israel in a binding oath, and Jeremiah had said the day would come when people would swear by the LORD who brought them out of the land of the north, not out of Egypt (16:14–15; 23:7–8). Here the opposite is threatened: no Judean in Egypt will use his name again. It is not a ban on speech but a promise that the community will not last.

a: keeping watch over them
p: The word is shoqed, 'watching', from Jeremiah's call vision of the almond branch.
b: In his call vision Jeremiah saw an almond branch (shaqed) and heard the LORD say he was "watching" (shoqed) over his word to do it (1:11–12). Here the same verb returns, now for harm and not for good. The Plain English Translation keeps the same English verb. In 31:28 the LORD watched to tear down and will watch to build. The wordplay gives the book's beginning and the end of its narrative a common phrase.

a: whose word stands: mine or theirs
p: The final test is the one the Law gave: whose word comes true.
b: Deuteronomy 18:21–22 says the sign of a true prophet is that his word happens. Jeremiah had said the same to Hananiah (28:9). Here the contest is not between two prophets but between God and the whole remnant of Judah, and the proof will come only later, in Egypt. The few who escape the sword and return will serve as witnesses. In the Greek the phrase "mine or theirs" is missing; see the variant. Isaiah 40:8, which says the word of our God stands forever, is the positive form of the same truth.

a: Pharaoh Hophra
p: Hophra is the Egyptian king Wahibre (Apries), who ruled 589–570 BC and was overthrown by his general Amasis.
b: Hophra, Greek Apries, marched against Babylon's siege of Jerusalem and withdrew (Jeremiah 37:5–11), and Herodotus says he fought Tyre and Sidon (Histories 2.161). His army, sent against Cyrene, was beaten and revolted; the Egyptians made his general Amasis king, and after a civil war Hophra died, strangled, according to Herodotus (2.161–169). The dating is about 570 BC for his fall and about 567 for his death. This matches "handed over to enemies who are after his life" in outline; Jeremiah does not name Amasis, and some readers hold that the verse points to Babylon instead. Ezekiel 29–32 has other oracles on this Pharaoh.

a: in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah
t: A word dated nineteen years early
p: The dated word of chapter 45 comes from 605 BC, but it stands after the fall of Jerusalem.
b: The date is the fourth year of Jehoiakim, 605/604 BC, the year Baruch wrote the first scroll (36:1–4) and Babylon won at Carchemish. Chapter 45 is placed last in the story of Jeremiah's life, not in time order, and the Greek puts it at the same point (followed there by chapter 52). Three explanations: it is Baruch's own seal on the story (Baruch the author of the stories, as some argue); it frames chapters 26–45 with the scroll of 36; or it was set here to close the book's first main part before the oracles on the nations. The word is also a kind of end to the story of Jeremiah's circle: the one who wrote down the words gets his own.

a: piled sorrow on top of my pain
p: Baruch's complaint uses Jeremiah's own words for sorrow.
b: "Sorrow" is yagon, used in Jeremiah's laments: "Why was I born, to see toil and sorrow?" (20:18; also 8:18; 31:13). "Worn out with groaning" matches the lament of Psalm 6:6. Baruch, after years of copying and carrying Jeremiah's words, is worn out by them. The LORD does not scold him; he tells him the larger picture (45:4–5).

a: What I have built I am about to demolish, and what I have planted I am about to pull up
p: The four verbs of the call, run backward. It is the LORD's own work that is being undone.
b: The verbs return from 1:10 and 42:10 in the same English. What is new here is the first person: it is "what I have built" and "what I have planted," the LORD's own work, that he is tearing down. The scribe's grief is a small thing next to that. The same thought is in Isaiah 5:1–7, where the owner of the vineyard pulls down its wall, and in Jeremiah 12:15, where after uprooting he will have compassion again.

a: do you go on seeking great things for yourself?
p: Readers disagree on what Baruch wanted: status, safety or a place in the new order.
b: The Hebrew gedolot, "great things," is open. Readers have suggested the prestige of a royal scribe in the circle of Shaphan's family, for whom Gemariah served as a high official (36:10); a future in the restored kingdom; or simply safety and rest. The LORD's offer is not a position but his life as loot (compare 39:18), which carries the thought that safety in a falling world is itself a gift. Later books were written in his name: Baruch (Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox churches; Protestants and Jews do not count it) and 2 Baruch (in no church's canon).
